summary: A stopped server now says it is stopped instead of claiming its host is offline
Restart and shutdown notices reach players within seconds instead of after the shutdown had already finished
A session whose byte stream lost data is refused instead of resumed, so an edge restart ends in a clean disconnect rather than a protocol error
Shutdown logs whether a sibling edge exists to take the players over; with none, open sessions will drop and the log now says so
On restart the edge now says whether the splice can actually move players to a sibling, and names why a sibling was unusable
The splice sidecar no longer reports itself as permanently unhealthy; it was answering the edge's health probe, which it never serves

Players are no longer disconnected when the edge they are routed through restarts; the player-to-server direction is now resent after a failover instead of being lost. Takes effect once the pinned splice image is moved to the current splice tag
The node now tracks how much player data the Minecraft server actually received, so an edge failover can resume the connection exactly where it left off

An edge restart no longer disconnects players immediately: if the first edge the session moves to cannot complete the handover, the splice now tries the next one and falls back to the previous behaviour instead of ending the session

An edge restart no longer ends in a connection reset: a failed handover now disconnects cleanly and the player reconnects, instead of resuming the session with missing data that the Minecraft server rejects
Edge restarts no longer disconnect players: the handover was miscounting the connection handshake, so it rejected every resume as damaged even when nothing was lost
Edge logs stay readable during a failover on a busy server: per-player lines are now grouped into one line per event with a count, instead of one line per player
After an edge goes down the splice no longer moves players back to it too early, which caused a second unnecessary handover per restart

The tunnel agent now offers Core and Redis on two local ports and keeps the real addresses up to date itself, so a machine on your hardware survives a platform address change with a few retries instead of a manual edit
Tunnel agent status lines (applied commands, rejected settings, bad input) now appear in the container log instead of only in a place nothing reads
An unreachable platform address no longer makes the tunnel agent ask the platform for a new one back to back; it now waits between attempts

An edge failover can no longer hand a player a stream with a gap in it: one of the two paths that buffer server output during the handover dropped data silently when it filled up, so the session was resumed as if nothing was lost and the Minecraft client failed with a packet error instead of reconnecting

A server stopped because its storage quota is full now tells players exactly that, instead of reporting the host as offline; the host was never the problem and the message pointed everyone at the wrong thing

A route whose target port fell outside 1-65535 was accepted and stored, then silently ignored by every edge, so the domain was simply dead with nothing logged; such a route is now rejected and the reason recorded.

A queued routing change the hub could not process without crashing brought the hub down and was put back at the front of the queue on restart, so it crashed again on every start with no way out; such a message is now dropped with the reason recorded instead.
Updated the Postgres driver, which carried a memory-safety bug and mishandled dollar-quoted strings in a way that could change how a query was parsed.
The route-only link's status endpoint now really binds to loopback. It was given a host:port value that the code turned into an invalid address, so the endpoint silently never started.
The tunnel interface is now named dylaris-wg0 instead of wg0, so it can no longer take over a WireGuard interface you already run. If you pinned WG_INTERFACE to wg0, change it to dylaris-wg0.

A machine whose overlay address is reassigned - which happens when a suspension is lifted - now picks the new address up within half a minute. It used to keep the old one, so the tunnel handshaked and reported healthy on both ends while nothing got through, until the ten-minute re-enrol repaired it.
Upgrading past the interface rename now removes the old wg0 tunnel it left behind, but only when its key proves it was ours. A WireGuard interface you set up yourself is never touched.

The hub admin UI can now create and delete routes, not just list them. Pick the link a route should reach from a dropdown of your links by name, give it a domain and a target address. This is what lets a gateway be run on its own, without a panel in front of it.

Links can now be created and deleted in the hub admin UI. Name a link, copy its token onto the machine that runs it, then point routes at it by that name. Deleting a link that routes still use is refused and tells you how many.
